title: Edges and merges — Image Wiki
text:
Edges and merges
  Where two areas meet, and what happens when they meet badly. An edge you cannot find is a tool when it was intended and a defect when it was not.

  
    Termedges / mergers
    Also calledlost edges, hard and soft edges, tangents, mergers, kissing edges
    Not the same assharpness and focus, outline as a drawn line, hard and soft light
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        An edge is not a lineHard, soft, lostWhy touching things fuseThe frame's own edgeCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Put a black phone down on a black table and step back three metres. You know there is a phone there. You cannot see one. The phone did not get smaller or darker or blurrier — it lost its outline, and an object with no findable outline is not an object any more.
Everything in a picture is bounded by edges of that kind, and two separate questions come out of it. What are the edges inside the frame like — crisp, soft, or gone? And what happens where things run into the frame's own edge? They belong in one article because they have one mechanism underneath them.
An edge is not a line
Smarthistory's definition of a shape is exact and easy to skip past: a shape is bounded by a line around it, or by a change in colour (SRC-008). In a drawing you get the line. In a photograph you never do. Every edge in a photograph is a change — in value, in hue, in texture, in sharpness — and if the change is not there, neither is the shape.
Which means an edge has two independent properties, and mixing them up causes most of the confusion in this topic:

How big the step is. A large step gives a strong edge, a small step a weak one, and no step gives nothing.
How wide the transition is. A step can happen over one pixel or over a finger's width.

Those are different dials. A soft edge can be a huge step spread over a wide band; a hard edge can be a tiny step made abruptly. Softness comes from the light (Hard and soft light) or the lens; the size of the step comes from what the two areas are.
Hard, soft, lost

Hard edgea bare bulb, midday sunyou could trace the whole outlineSoft edgea big window, an overcast skythe outline is a band, not a lineLost edgethe shadow side against a wall of its own valuethe right-hand outline is not there at all

Same form, same position, same background in all three panels — a light wall on the left and a wall in shadow on the right. Only the form's own rendering changes.
Hard: a big step made abruptly. You could trace the whole outline with a pencil. Soft: the same step spread over a band, so the outline is no longer a line and there is nowhere exact to put the pencil. Lost: the step against the right-hand wall has gone to zero, because the form is now that wall's value. The dashes mark a contour that is genuinely not in the picture — and note that the left-hand contour still reads perfectly, because that boundary still has a step.
One form can carry all three at once. Most good painting does.





Diego Velázquez, Juan de Pareja, 1650 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
All three edge qualities in one head, and you can find each of them in about five seconds.
Hard: the white collar against the dark doublet. A traceable zigzag, the crispest boundary in the painting, and it sits directly under the face — which is where Velázquez wanted you.
Soft: the top and right of the hair against the grey wall. There is a boundary, but it takes a finger's width to happen, and if you try to say exactly where the hair ends you cannot.
Lost: the lower left. His shoulder and cloak are the same value as the ground behind them and the contour is simply absent — the figure has no left-hand outline below the shoulder at all. Nothing is wrong with the picture. The edges that survived are the ones that describe the face, and the ones that were given up were describing a sleeve.


The difference between a lost edge that works and one that ruins a photograph is not the edge. It is whether the surviving edges still describe the thing the picture is about. Velázquez gave up a sleeve. A photographer who lets a dark jacket dissolve into a dark doorway has given up the person.
Why touching things fuse
Grouping runs on the flat array of pixels, before anything is recognised and before depth is worked out. Two regions of similar value that touch get consolidated into one area — that is not a metaphor, it is the stated priority of the machinery: find edges, use them as the borders of areas, then reduce the variation inside each area and raise the contrast between areas (SRC-064). Continuity carries a line straight through whatever interrupts it, and closure finishes the shape (SRC-028).
None of that has access to the fact that the pole is thirty metres behind the head. It has two dark patches with no step between them, and two dark patches with no step between them are one patch.

A clear gapdark pole, a head's width awaytwo objects: a person, and a post behindTouchingdark pole, same value, now grazingone object: the post grows out of the headTouching, different valuea whitewashed post in exactly the same placetwo objects again: the outline survives

Left to right, two things change one at a time, and both are necessary for the merge.
Panel 1 to panel 2: only the post's position moves. With a clear gap you see a person and a post behind them. Grazing the outline, the two dark shapes consolidate and the post appears to grow out of the head.
Panel 2 to panel 3: the post stays in exactly the same place and only its value changes. A whitewashed post in the identical position does not merge with anything, because there is now a step across the boundary.
So a merge needs adjacency and similar value together. Adjacency alone is harmless, which is why "keep things away from each other" is the wrong lesson and "watch what shares a value with what" is the right one.


The famous cases are all the same case. A lamp post growing out of a head: a dark vertical touching a dark head. A horizon slicing a neck: a long horizontal crossing a shape at a place where its two sides happen to match in value. Two people in a group shot fusing into one lump: two dark suits, shoulder to shoulder, with nothing between them. You do not need to memorise the list. You need to check what touches what, and whether the two things that touch are the same tone.


The full frame: a loaded truck, three men, a boy climbing, a utility pole
Our own detail of the three men against the cab


Jack Delano, French-Canadian potato farmers near Caribou, Maine, October 1940. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress; public domain. The right panel is our own crop of the left one.
A real photograph, by a very good photographer, with real merges in it — the ordinary kind rather than the cartoon kind.
In the detail, find the outline of the man in the middle. Down his right side, around his raised arm and over his shoulder there is nothing to find: his dark jacket and the truck's dark cab are the same value and the boundary between them does not exist. What rescues him is three small hard edges — the pale glove up at the wing mirror, the checked shirt, the light collar. Cover those with a fingertip and he loses his shape. The seated man on the right is in the same position: his shoulder merges into the cab, and his pale hat is doing all the separating.
In the full frame, look at the utility pole on the right. Its foot disappears behind the boy climbing the tailboard, so pole and boy read as one dark upright, and the pole then runs off the top edge and takes the eye with it. That is the tangent the textbooks describe, found in the wild rather than staged.


The frame's own edge
The border is a hard, straight, maximum-contrast line, so everything above applies to it too — with two extra consequences.
A shape that just touches the border merges with it and reads as attached to the frame rather than sitting inside the picture. A clear gap works. A decisive overlap works. The half-measure is what fails: a peak that nearly grazes the top edge draws attention away from everything else in the frame (SRC-017).
A shape that runs off the edge is an exit. Your eye follows it out, and there is nothing out there to come back for — which is why photographers put a branch or a wall at the border, to close the composition rather than decorate it (SRC-021). A bright road or a strong diagonal leaving through a corner is the usual culprit.
Common mistakes

"A soft edge means the photo is out of focus." Focus is one cause. Soft light, distance haze, motion and a painter's brush are others, and an image can be perfectly sharp with every edge soft.
"A lost edge is always a mistake." It is the main way painters keep attention where they want it. Ask which edges survived before you call it a fault.
"The background is obviously behind the subject, so nobody will be confused." Grouping happens before understanding. Once the pole is coming out of the head, explaining the geometry changes nothing (Gestalt grouping).
"Cluttered backgrounds cause mergers." Value similarity causes mergers. A plain wall the same tone as a coat is worse than a busy wall in a different tone.
"Different colours will keep the shapes apart." Only if they differ in value. A mid-red jacket against a mid-green hedge is a lost edge in waiting (Value structure).


Reading the edges of an image

Trace the subject's outline with your eye, all the way round. Where does it disappear?
At each disappearance, ask what is on the other side and whether it shares the subject's value.
Decide whether the edges that survived still describe the subject. If they only describe a sleeve, the merge is a defect.
Walk the four borders. Anything just touching, or leaving through a corner?
Squint or shrink the image. Mergers get worse at small sizes, which is the size most people will see it at.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Gestalt grouping
              The automatic machinery that turns a field of pixels into objects and groups — and the reason accidental alignments in a photograph look deliberate.
            
          
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hard and soft light
              Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.
            
          
        
          
            
              Framing and cropping
              The frame is a decision about what is in the picture and what is not. The crop is the cheapest powerful edit there is — which also makes it the easiest way to throw the subject away.
